title: The Gabbai's Grandson: Belz to the Second Avenue Rialto by way of Vilna, Buenos Aires and Johannesburg
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Court at Belz and the House in Leopoldstadt

stops.name: Belz, the gabbai's grandson is born
stops.date_confidence: Year probable, day and month unestablished. Most institutional sources give 1907, consistent with the age of about fifty-four reported at his death; Brigitte Dalinger's research is cited for an alternative estimate of about 1900. No birth record has been produced in any source consulted, and the two years are left standing against each other.
stops.campa: In Belz in eastern Galicia, a small town under the Habsburgs whose name the Hasidic world knows better than any atlas does, a son is born into a family attached to the rebbe's court. His grandfather is R' Ira Lokman, head gabbai to the Belzer rebbe, the man who controls the door. The child will spend his working life on stages his grandfather would have shut, singing in the language the court spoke at table. Two birth years circulate and nothing in the record chooses between them.
stops.quote: His grandfather, R' Ira Lokman, was the head gabbai (sexton).
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The court of the Belzer rebbe at Belz, Lviv Oblast, the household his grandfather kept the door of
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3 (1959), English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
David Assaf, Oneg Shabbat, 14 March 2014
Brigitte Dalinger, Verloschene Sterne: Geschichte des judischen Theaters in Wien (cited, not retrieved)

stops.name: Vienna, Leopoldstadt and the transplanted court
stops.date_confidence: Approximate. Zylbercweig gives his age as six without naming a year, which puts the move at about 1913 if the 1907 birth holds; Dalinger is cited for an arrival in 1914. Both figures are reported. No document of the family's registration in Vienna was located.
stops.campa: The family leaves Galicia for Vienna and settles in Leopoldstadt, the island quarter across the canal where Galician Jews arrive by the trainload. He is six years old, or thereabouts. The upbringing is strict and Hasidic and continues as though the move had changed nothing: prayer, study, the court's discipline transplanted whole into an imperial capital with an opera house in it. Outside the door, Vienna is playing operetta in four theaters at once.
suggested_refs: The Galician Jewish quarter of Leopoldstadt, Vienna, before the First World War
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
Brigitte Dalinger, Verloschene Sterne (cited, not retrieved)

stops.name: Vienna, the Freie Judische Volksbuhne and the name that is not his
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by Zylbercweig and by Wikipedia, which dates the engagement 1919 to 1922. Coordinate is a Leopoldstadt placement for the company, not a confirmed street address; no source consulted gives the hall it used.
stops.campa: At twelve he walks into the Freie Judische Volksbuhne and is taken in by Itzhak Deutsch. He acts under a name that is not his own, because the name that is his own belongs to the gabbai's grandson and cannot appear on a Vienna playbill. For three years, to 1922, he keeps two lives: the boy at the court's prayers and the boy in the wings. The pseudonyms have not survived. No source consulted records a single one of them, and the family's discovery of the second life is nowhere dated.
stops.quote: joined secretly under a pen-name the « Jewish Free Theatre » at the age of 12
stops.quote_source: Institut Europeen des Musiques Juives, 'Witler, Ben-Zion (1907-1961)'
suggested_refs: The Freie Judische Volksbuhne (Fraye Yidishe Folks-Bine) of Vienna, founded in the immediate postwar years
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
Institut Europeen des Musiques Juives (IEMJ), biographical entry

stops.name: Vienna, the Wiener Morgenzeitung and four years off the stage
stops.date_confidence: Attested twice, by Wikipedia and by Zylbercweig, though both describe the paper wrongly as a weekly. The German Wikipedia article on the Wiener Morgenzeitung establishes it as a daily running from 19 January 1919 to 17 September 1927, which caps the episode. The exact year he joined it is not given; 1922 is taken from Wikipedia's dating of the end of his first Volksbuhne run.
stops.campa: Family pressure closes the wings to him. He takes a place at the Wiener Morgenzeitung, Robert Stricker's German-language Zionist paper, and becomes a contributor: a young man with a trained voice writing copy in a newsroom. Both his biographers call the paper a weekly and both are wrong, since it appeared daily from January 1919 until it folded in September 1927. Four years pass this way, and he is nineteen when he goes back to the theater. Not one article signed by him has been located.
stops.quote: He worked briefly as a journalist at the German Zionist weekly Wiener Morgenzeitung (Vienna Morning Times), but in 1926 returned to the Vienna theater scene
suggested_refs: The Wiener Morgenzeitung, Robert Stricker's Zionist daily, Vienna 1919-1927
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
German Wikipedia, 'Wiener Morgenzeitung'

stops.name: Vienna, Praterstrasse and the house with Goldflus
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Zylbercweig gives 1926 for the return and the Praterstrasse opening with I. Goldflus; Dalinger is cited for an opening of the company in autumn 1927 with Witler appearing in 1928. Both figures are reported. The company name Di Yidishe Kinstler Shpile comes from Zylbercweig, not from Wikipedia, which says only that he returned to the Vienna theater scene.
stops.campa: He returns to the stage and opens a house with I. Goldflus, in Sholem Asch's Unzer gloybn. The company is remembered under the name Di Yidishe Kinstler Shpile. He is playing comedies and operettas now, not the repertory of conviction his family might in the end have forgiven, and the argument at home is finished. The Praterstrasse is Leopoldstadt's spine, running from the canal to the fairground, and the Jewish theaters sit along it among the cafes, one house after another.
stops.quote: In 1926 he again returned to the theatre and opened, together with I. Goldflus in Vienna on Praterstrasse.
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The Judische Kunstlerspiele on the Praterstrasse, Vienna's interwar Yiddish house
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
Brigitte Dalinger, Verloschene Sterne (cited, not retrieved)

stops.name: Vienna, the professors Ulianowsky and Fuks
stops.date_confidence: Attested in both Zylbercweig and Wikipedia, which names the teachers as Yulianovsky and Fuchs. Neither source dates the lessons; 1927 orders them between the 1926 return and the tour that begins in September 1928.
stops.campa: He puts himself under two voice teachers, Ulianowsky and Fuks, whose names Wikipedia gives as Yulianovsky and Fuchs, and studies opera repertoire in a city that takes such study seriously. What comes out of it is not an opera singer. It is a Yiddish operetta lead, a man who can carry a house on a melody and a joke in the same breath, trained by professors who thought they were making something else. Neither source dates the lessons. Within a year he is working outside Austria.
stops.quote: W. got to studying singing with the professors Ulianowsky and Fuks and went over to operetta repertoire.
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: Vienna's private voice studios of the 1920s, where operetta leads were trained on opera repertory
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Riga, the season with Etta Topol that the source cannot place
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, unresolved. The English adaptation of Zylbercweig's entry gives a Riga guest engagement with the prima donna Etta Topol in 1927, which in the same entry falls before the Vienna return it also dates to 1926 and describes as coming first. Either the year is a transcription error for 1937 or the engagement is genuinely this early. The date here orders the stop where the source puts it; the coordinate is the canonical Riga pin.
stops.campa: A Riga guest engagement with the prima donna Etta Topol appears in the record here, dated 1927, ahead of the Vienna return that the same page describes as coming first. Either he crossed the Baltic before he had finished his training, or a compositor set a seven where a three belonged and this is the season he plays eleven years later with a different partner. Riga will matter to him either way, and the record does not say from when. The source contradicts itself and does not notice.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish theatre companies of interwar Riga and their visiting prima donnas
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Paris, the guest circuit opens
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Zylbercweig gives September 1928 as the start of the run and Wikipedia lists the same destinations. Coordinate is the canonical Paris pin; no Paris theater is named in any source consulted and no address survives.
stops.campa: In September he begins a guest circuit that will run two years. Paris first, where the Yiddish-speaking emigration fills halls for singers who arrive with a Vienna reputation behind them. He is twenty-one and travelling on his voice alone, with a booking sheet and no company of his own. Western Europe out and back again is the shape of it, and he will keep working that shape under other flags and across other oceans. No theater is named in any source consulted and no address survives; only the city and the month.
stops.quote: He performed from September 1928 until 1930 in Paris, London, South Africa, and further in London, France and Vienna.
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The Yiddish-speaking quarters of interwar Paris and their guest-star bookings
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: London, Whitechapel and the first English season
stops.date_confidence: Attested as part of the 1928-1930 circuit by both Zylbercweig and Wikipedia; the year within that span is not given and 1929 orders the stop. Coordinate marks the historic Whitechapel Yiddish theatre district, not a confirmed venue.
stops.campa: He guest-stars in London, in the East End, where the Yiddish theater of the English-speaking world keeps its houses along Whitechapel Road. No playbill with his name on it has been recovered from this visit; the record holds the fact and nothing more. Whitechapel is one of the first places he plays where the audience speaks his language and the street outside does not, and he will come back to it twice, once in a plan the German army cancels and once, twenty-one years on, with a wife and a joint billing.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish playhouses of Whitechapel Road, London, in the years before the war
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Johannesburg, the first South African leg
stops.date_confidence: Attested as South Africa within the 1928-1930 circuit; no city, theater, or date is named in any source consulted. Johannesburg city-centre coordinates are a placement on the strength of it being the country's Yiddish theatrical centre, not a confirmed location.
stops.campa: The circuit runs south to South Africa, further than a Yiddish company had any commercial reason to go. He learns on this leg that Yiddish audiences exist anywhere Jews have settled in numbers and that he can reach them; he will be back on the same ground in 1955, with a troupe out of Buenos Aires. Which city he played, which theater, and how he got there the record does not say. Johannesburg is the reasonable guess, and the guess is all there is.
suggested_refs: The South African Yiddish theatrical circuit between the wars
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Vienna, the loop closes
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Vienna is the last destination named in Zylbercweig's list of the 1928-1930 circuit and Wikipedia's independent list ends the same way. No venue is given for the return engagement.
stops.campa: The tour closes where it began. Zylbercweig's line runs Paris, London, South Africa, and further in London, France and Vienna, and Vienna is the last word in it: the circuit is a loop and the loop comes home. He is twenty-three, a guest star with three continents behind him and no company of his own to put them in. Austria is still a country in which a Jewish actor can work a full season. He has nine years left to get out of Europe and no reason yet to count them.
suggested_refs: Vienna's Yiddish stage at the turn of the 1930s, before the Austrofascist and Nazi years
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Vilna, the letter to the editor
stops.date_confidence: Attested by date through Zylbercweig's contemporary-press bibliography, which lists a letter to the editor in Di tsayt on 14 November 1933 and N. Linder's theater feuilleton in the Vilner tog on 17 November. Neither text has been read by anyone working from the bibliography. Coordinate is the former Jewish quarter of Vilnius; the city-centre pin is 54.6872, 25.2797.
stops.campa: He arrives in Vilna and the Yiddish press takes him up at once. On the fourteenth of November his letter to the editor runs in Di tsayt; three days later N. Linder gives him a theater feuilleton in the Vilner tog. A visiting operetta lead who writes to the papers and gets printed is settling into a town rather than passing through it. The letters themselves have not been read by anyone working from these bibliographies. Only their dates and their existence are on record.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish daily press of Vilna: Di tsayt and the Vilner tog, 1933-1935
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, contemporary-press bibliography, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Warsaw, Smocza Street and the Eldorado
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, unresolved. Benny Mer names Witler among the performers at the Eldorado on Smocza Street, which puts him in Warsaw; a 2007 Jewish Currents piece on his song Varshe states that he never saw the city he wrote about. The Mer article was fetched and read directly; the Jewish Currents piece was not located. Neither claim is dated to a year, and 1934 orders the stop inside the Polish years. Coordinate is an approximate Warsaw placement, not the Smocza Street address.
stops.campa: On Smocza Street in the Warsaw Jewish quarter stands the Eldorado, and Benny Mer's reconstruction of that street names him among those who played, danced and sang there. Against this stands a claim published in 2007 that Witler never saw the city he wrote about, the city of his song Varshe. Both cannot be true. He spends three years touring Poland in this decade, and he writes Krokhmalne gas about a Warsaw street in the first person, as a man saying where he was born. The record leaves the contradiction standing.
stops.quote: Krokhmalne Street, you are dear to me, have a special place in my heart, I would stretch out my neck for you and let them chop off my head.
stops.quote_source: 'Krokhmalne gas,' English translation, The Yosl and Chana Mlotek Yiddish Song Collection, yiddishsongs.org
suggested_refs: The Eldorado theatre on Smocza Street, Warsaw, and the songs Varshe and Krokhmalne gas
sources: Benny Mer, 'Reimagining the Lively Character of Pre-War Smocza Street,' The Forward, 2 May 2017
The Yosl and Chana Mlotek Yiddish Song Collection, 'Krokhmalne gas,' yiddishsongs.org
Jewish Currents, 2007 piece on the song 'Varshe' (cited, not located)

stops.name: Vilna, master of the Yiddish operetta
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Zylbercweig's bibliography item reads 'L. S-ki -- Ben zion vitler der meyster fun der yidisher operete, same, 10 November 1935,' and the chain of 'same' references runs back to Di tsayt of Vilna, correcting the dossier's placement of the piece in an unnamed Polish paper. The article itself has not been read.
stops.campa: Under the byline L. S-ki, Di tsayt of Vilna prints a profile headed Ben zion vitler der meyster fun der yidisher operete. He is twenty-eight and the Yiddish press of Lithuania has decided what he is: not a comic, not a singer, the master of the form. Two years of Vilna press items sit in the bibliography between his first letter to an editor and this profile, and every one of them is about him. Zylbercweig's own phrase for these Polish years is that he became the darling of the public.
stops.quote_source: Institut Europeen des Musiques Juives, 'Witler, Ben-Zion (1907-1961)'
suggested_refs: Zylbercweig's contemporary-press bibliography for Witler, items 1 to 5, Vilna 1933-1935
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, contemporary-press bibliography, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Institut Europeen des Musiques Juives (IEMJ), biographical entry
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Pinsk, the visit to the orphanage
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig's bibliography, which cites Unzer pinsker leben for 1936, including a separate item on his call at a Jewish orphanage in the city. Month not given. The orphanage is not named and the articles have not been retrieved.
stops.campa: Unzer pinsker leben covers his visit to the city, and covers, in a separate item, his call at a Jewish orphanage there. The orphanage is not named. The occasion is not given. What the bibliography records is that a touring operetta star went to see children who had nobody and that the local paper thought it worth a column. Pinsk is the last stop in the Polish press record. After November 1936 the items stop, and the next thing the record shows is him moving north to the Baltic.
suggested_refs: Unzer pinsker leben, the Yiddish paper of Pinsk, 1936
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, contemporary-press bibliography, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

segments.name: The Baltic Season and the Border Closing

stops.name: Riga, the season with Nina Talina
stops.date_confidence: Contested date. Zylbercweig states flatly that in 1938 he played Riga with the prima donna Nina Talina, and the seven-title repertory comes from him alone. Wikipedia gives 1937 for a Riga appearance and names a different repertoire, A Khasene in Shtetl and The Galitzian Wedding by William Siegel, without mentioning Talina. Dalinger is cited for a major Latvian season of 1937-1938 and for the birth of a son there; her text was not retrieved. Canonical Riga pin.
stops.campa: He plays a Riga season with the prima donna Nina Talina: A shpil in libe, The Folk Singer, Kinder fargesn nit, A khasene in shtetl, Eltern un kinder, Der nayer yid, S'vet zayn got. Seven titles in one engagement, the working repertory of a man who can open anything on a week's notice. Dalinger's research records that a son is born to him in Latvia during this stay. The child's name is not recovered. The mother is not named. Nothing further about the boy appears in any source consulted.
stops.quote: In 1938 he played in Riga, where he performed (together with the prima donna Nina Talina).
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The Riga Yiddish theatre season of 1937-1938 and the career of Nina Talina
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
Brigitte Dalinger, Verloschene Sterne (cited, not retrieved)

stops.name: Kovno, the summer engagement
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig as a summer engagement following the Riga season; no theater and no exact dates are given. The month is an ordering device for 'summer'.
stops.campa: After Riga he takes the summer in Kovno, the provisional capital, where the Yiddish theater keeps a season running through the warm months. No theater is named. Riga in the winter and Kovno for the summer is the standard shape of a Baltic year for a Yiddish star of this decade, worked by many and remarked on by nobody. It is the last engagement he is recorded playing on ground that will be taken and emptied within four years, and he plays it as an ordinary summer job. He is thirty-one.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish summer season in Kovno (Kaunas), capital of independent Lithuania
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Poland, the company and the invitation to Harry Ariel
stops.date_confidence: The invitation is attested verbatim by David Mazower for the summer of 1939, and Ariel's passport-office appointment for the morning of 2 September 1939 is his. Witler's own whereabouts in that summer are not documented in any source consulted; the pin marks the Polish touring circuit where his company was working, per the Monash biographical archive entry on Shmuel Migdalek, which was not independently retrieved.
stops.campa: He is running his own travelling company now, the Ben Zion Witler Travelling Acting Company, working the Polish circuit. In the summer he offers a young Polish actor, Harry Ariel, the juvenile light comedian's place in a company he means to open in London. Ariel applies for a visa and a first Polish passport and plans to call at the passport office on the morning of the second of September. The invasion reaches him that day. Ariel flees east, survives Soviet labour camps and gets to England in 1948. The London company never assembles.
stops.quote: In the summer of 1939, Benzion Witler invited him to join his company in London as the "juvenile light comedian."
stops.quote_source: David Mazower, 'Zylbercweig's Leksikon and Selfridges' Rump Steak: In Memoriam Harry Ariel,' Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 5 July 2018
suggested_refs: The Ben Zion Witler Travelling Acting Company of prewar Poland, which the child actor Shmuel Migdalek joined
sources: David Mazower, Digital Yiddish Theatre Project, 5 July 2018
Monash University biographical archive, entry on Shmuel Migdalek (cited, not retrieved)
Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

segments.name: America, and Starting Over in the Provinces

stops.name: Brooklyn, the Hopkinson Theatre in Brownsville
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikipedia and Zylbercweig both give the Hopkinson Theatre engagement in Fargesene froyen for October 1940, and Zylbercweig's bibliography cites W. Edlin's review in Der Tog on 20 October 1940, which was not independently retrieved. His route out of Europe is documented nowhere.
stops.campa: He is in Brooklyn, in Brownsville, at the Hopkinson Theatre, in William Siegel's Fargesene froyen. How he got out of Europe is not documented anywhere: no ship, no port, no visa, no date of crossing. Brownsville is a long way from the Vilner tog and from the houses of the Praterstrasse, and it is where the work is. The young actor he was writing to the summer before is behind a line he crossed and Ariel did not. The record picks him up already on this side, opening a play in October, and W. Edlin reviews it in Der Tog on the twentieth.
suggested_refs: The Hopkinson Theatre, Brownsville, Brooklyn, one of the outer-borough Yiddish houses
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Cleveland, the provincial circuit
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig, who names Cleveland and states that he toured further American provincial cities. No theater and no month are given, and no review has been located.
stops.campa: He works Cleveland and the American provincial circuit, the towns with a Yiddish audience and no permanent company: a week here, a fortnight there, the same handful of plays carried in trunks. The star of the Vilna press is touring stock now, in cities he had not heard of two years earlier, learning American distances, and he is thirty-four. No theater is named in the record for Cleveland and no review has been located. Zylbercweig gives the city, the word further, and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The American provincial Yiddish theatrical circuit of the early 1940s
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Chicago, A goldener khoylem at the Douglas Park Theatre
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Zylbercweig's bibliography cites a Forward review of A goldener khoylem at the Douglas Park Theatre on 6 March 1942, and Wikipedia gives the same engagement. The coordinate is approximate: the theatre stood on the West Ogden Avenue frontage west of Douglas Park, near the 3500 block, and no street address for it was recovered. Cinema Treasures has no entry.
stops.campa: At the Douglas Park Theatre on the west side he stages William Siegel's A goldener khoylem, and the Chicago Forward reviews it on the sixth of March. The house stands on the Ogden Avenue frontage west of the park; no street address for it has been recovered and its exact place on the block is guesswork. Chicago is the first American city that holds him. Under the managers Oscar Ostroff and Moshe Nestor he stays on, month after month, playing to a west-side Jewish public that keeps filling the seats.
suggested_refs: The Douglas Park Theatre, West Ogden Avenue, Chicago, and its Yiddish seasons of 1942-1943
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, contemporary-press bibliography, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Chicago, Home Sweet Home and a second season
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Zylbercweig's bibliography item 12 reads 'Sh. Zmd -- "Heym, zise heym," geshpilt in doglas park teater, "Forward," Chicago, 1 May 1942,' and item 13 records Wm. Siegel on Der heyliker tants at the same theater on 12 October 1943, extending the association into a second year. Coordinate approximate, as above.
stops.campa: Harry Kalmanowitz's Home Sweet Home, also called Motl the Peddler, goes up at the Douglas Park and the Forward reviews it on the first of May. The play will follow him: it anchors his first Buenos Aires season four years later and stays in the repertory after that. Two seasons in one house is the longest he has stood still since Vienna. The Chicago association runs on into the next year, with Wm. Siegel writing up Der heyliker tants at the same theater on the twelfth of October 1943.
suggested_refs: Harry Kalmanowitz's Home Sweet Home (Motl the Peddler), carried from Chicago to Buenos Aires
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, contemporary-press bibliography, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: New York, the Sun label and the Second Avenue studios
stops.date_confidence: Attested as recordings; undated as sessions. The George Blood digitizations on the Internet Archive carry label, catalogue and matrix data but no recording or issue year, the only year in the metadata being the 2022 digitization. Sun-label Yiddish discs belong to the 1940s and early 1950s, and 1945 is an ordering placement inside that span. Coordinate marks the Second Avenue theatrical and recording district, not a confirmed studio address.
stops.campa: He records for the Sun label, in the district of Second Avenue where the Yiddish theaters and the studios sat within a few blocks of each other. Djonkoya and Warsaw are pressed as the two sides of one disc, catalogue 1055; Bialystok, 80 ehr - 70 zee, Rivkele and Praven a chassene follow, some of them with the Mendelsohn ensemble behind him. Half the titles are Polish city names, sung in New York by a man who will not see any of those cities again. No studio address survives on the labels and no session dates were cut into the discs.
stops.quote: Krokhmalne Street, I know it well, I was born there
stops.quote_source: 'Krokhmalne gas,' English translation, The Yosl and Chana Mlotek Yiddish Song Collection, yiddishsongs.org
suggested_refs: The Sun label 78s digitized in the Internet Archive's George Blood collection, identifiers gbia0420293, gbia0420294, gbia0446564, gbia0446565

segments.name: Buenos Aires and the Southern Circuit

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Teatro Mitre and Shifra Lerer
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Wikipedia and Zylbercweig for the year, repertory and venue; Zylbercweig's bibliography cites Shmuel Rozhansky's reviews in Di idishe tsaytung of 2 August 1946 and 13 July 1947, neither retrieved. The coordinate is contested: the geography record puts the Teatro Mitre in Balvanera at -34.6047, -58.4082 and a second record puts it in Monserrat at -34.6083, -58.3821, about 2.4 km apart. No street address for the house was established. The Balvanera pin is used for all four Argentine stops in this file so they do not scatter.
stops.campa: He crosses to Argentina and opens at the Teatro Mitre in Buenos Aires with Home Sweet Home, Wolf Herzog's Alts far dir and Moshe Rubin's Zing mayn folk. Shmuel Rozhansky reviews the debut in Di idishe tsaytung. In the company is an Argentine-born actress named Shifra Lerer, thirty years old, raised in this city and working in this language. From this season the two of them are a fixed pair on every playbill either one of them appears on for the next fifteen years.
suggested_refs: The Teatro Mitre, one of the commercial Yiddish houses of Buenos Aires alongside the Soleil, the Excelsior and the Ombu
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'
Wikipedia, 'Shifra Lerer'

stops.name: Montevideo, across the river
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig only as Uruguay within the postwar South American tour; no city, venue or date is named. Montevideo and the Barrio Sur Jewish quarter are a placement, not a confirmed location.
stops.campa: The season runs on across the Rio de la Plata to Montevideo, where the Jewish quarter in the Barrio Sur supports a Yiddish public of its own. No venue is named in the record, no month, and no notice in any Uruguayan paper has been located; Zylbercweig gives the country and stops. He is forty years old. From here the working year has a northern base and a southern circuit, Buenos Aires to Montevideo to Brazil and back up again, run on a schedule that has nothing to do with which hemisphere is in summer.
suggested_refs: The Barrio Sur Jewish quarter of Montevideo and its Yiddish audiences
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Sao Paulo, Bom Retiro and the Brazilian leg
stops.date_confidence: Attested only as Brazil. No Brazilian city or theater is named in any source consulted; Bom Retiro in Sao Paulo, the best-documented Yiddish theatrical neighbourhood in the country, is a placement made on that basis alone and should be read as approximate.
stops.campa: Brazil is named in the record and no city in it is, no theater and no date either. The audiences here arrived in the twenties and thirties and have been waiting a long time for somebody who sounds like where they came from; three countries now sit on one loop, in one language. Bom Retiro in Sao Paulo, the immigrant quarter where the Yiddish theater of Brazil kept its houses, is the reasonable placement, and it is placed here on that basis and no other.
suggested_refs: Bom Retiro, Sao Paulo, and the Yiddish theatrical life of Brazilian Jewish immigration
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

segments.name: The Partnership: Two Hemispheres on One Circuit

stops.name: New York, the Bronx Art Theatre
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The engagement in Zayn groyse libe at the Bronx Art Theatre appears in Zylbercweig's entry and was not independently confirmed elsewhere; no review was located and the theatre's address was not confirmed. The coordinate is an approximate Bronx placement.
stops.campa: Back in New York he appears at the Bronx Art Theatre in Zayn groyse libe, His Great Love. He is playing the Bronx rather than Second Avenue, which is where a good part of the Yiddish audience has moved; the Rialto is contracting and the work is out in the neighborhoods now, in houses that will not be there in fifteen years. The record for this engagement is thin: one line in a biographical lexicon, no review located, no address for the house confirmed, no run length.
suggested_refs: The Bronx Art Theatre and the outer-borough Yiddish stage of the late 1940s
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: London, the joint billing with Lerer
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig for August 1950; the house is described only as London's Yiddish folk theater and is not named. Zylbercweig's bibliography also cites a Katie Brown farewell piece in Yiddish lebn, London, of January-February 1955, which was not retrieved.
stops.campa: He and Lerer guest-star together in London's Yiddish folk theater, the first tour they are documented making as a pair on this side of the Atlantic. The house is not named in any source consulted. Twenty-two years after his first Whitechapel engagement he is back in the same district, no longer the young export out of Vienna, and the London public he plays to now has a hole in it the size of the Continent. Katie Brown will write him a farewell in the London paper Yiddish lebn, five years later.
suggested_refs: Yiddish lebn, London, January-February 1955, Katie Brown's farewell article
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
Wikipedia, 'Ben-Zion Witler'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, A roman fun eyn nakht at the Mitre
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, unresolved. Louis Freiman's theatrical biography specifies July 1951 for the Teatro Mitre production of A roman fun eyn nakht; Zylbercweig compresses the same trip into an August 1950 departure from London. The two datings have not been reconciled and neither primary text was retrieved. Coordinate as at the 1946 stop.
stops.campa: At the Teatro Mitre he stages Louis Freiman's A roman fun eyn nakht, a romance of one night, in two acts and twelve scenes, with Lerer opposite him. Freiman's own theatrical biography puts the production in July 1951; the lexicon compresses the same trip into August 1950, and the two dates have not been reconciled by anyone. From Buenos Aires the tour goes on to Uruguay and to Brazil, the same three-country loop, in the same order it took the first time.
suggested_refs: Louis Freiman's A roman fun eyn nakht, two acts and twelve scenes, Teatro Mitre
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: New York, the Public Theatre and Uncle Sam in Israel
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig alone. Wikipedia says nothing about the Public Theatre, Yablokoff, Ressler or this title; the dossier's attribution of the claim to Wikipedia is an error and is dropped here. Month not given. Coordinate is the canonical Second Avenue Rialto pin.
stops.campa: At the Public Theatre on Second Avenue he and Lerer appear in Herman Yablokoff's production of Benjamin Ressler's Onkl Sem in Yisroel, Uncle Sam in Israel. Yablokoff is the largest name in the American Yiddish theater and the billing is a joint one. After this production they tour as a unit and are reviewed as a unit, and whoever remembers either of them remembers one act. Zylbercweig is the only source for it: Wikipedia says nothing about the Public Theatre, about Yablokoff, or about this title.
stops.quote: In 1952 W. participated in new York's Public Theatre in Yablokoff's production of Ressler's "Uncle Sam in Israel."
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The Public Theatre on Second Avenue and Herman Yablokoff's productions of the early 1950s
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Mayn mans kale
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Zylbercweig's bibliography item 19 reads 'T. Belin [Dr. L. Zhitnitsky] -- "Mayn mans kale," "Di prese," Buenos Aires, 11 July 1953,' with a further notice over the initials Sh. R. on 1 August 1953. The title translates as My Husband's Bride, not My Husband's Wife. Neither review was retrieved. Coordinate as at the 1946 stop; no venue is named for this season.
stops.campa: He stages Mayn mans kale, My Husband's Bride, in Buenos Aires, and on the eleventh of July Di prese reviews it under the byline T. Belin, which is Dr. L. Zhitnitsky writing under another name. Three weeks later a second notice runs over the initials Sh. R. It is his fourth Argentine season in seven years, played to a public that by now regards him as one of its own, though he has never lived in the country for a full year. Neither review has been read by anyone working from the bibliography, and the house he played is not named in it either.
suggested_refs: Di prese and Di idishe tsaytung, the Yiddish dailies of Buenos Aires, and their theatre criticism
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, contemporary-press bibliography, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Montevideo, the 1953 continuation
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig as Uruguay and Brazil following the Argentine season; no city, venue or month is named. September is an ordering device placing the leg after the 11 July Buenos Aires review.
stops.campa: The Argentine season continues to Uruguay and to Brazil, as it did in 1946 and again in 1951. Zylbercweig's sentence for it is flat and unadorned, a tour across Argentina and from there to Uruguay and Brazil, with no venue in either country named. No month is given for the leg; the record holds only the countries and the order they came in. He is working the loop for the third time, and with a partner rather than alone. The biographer records it the way a timetable records a train.
stops.quote: In 1953 he again made a tour (with Shifra Lerer) across Argentina...and from there to Uruguay and Brazil
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires to Montevideo to Sao Paulo Yiddish touring loop of the 1940s and 1950s
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Johannesburg, the Technical College Theatre
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Zylbercweig, who names the year, the venue, the play and the fact that the troupe travelled from Argentina. Wikipedia mentions South Africa only in a blanket clause about the 1950s and names neither venue nor play; the dossier's attribution to Wikipedia is dropped. Month not given.
stops.campa: A troupe leaves Argentina for South Africa and he and Lerer are in it, playing H. Hoffenberg's Mayn gliklekhe heym at the Technical College Theatre in Johannesburg. It is the second time he has worked this ground. The first was a guest engagement somewhere in the country between 1928 and 1930, before he had a wife, a partner or a name outside Europe, and it left behind no venue, no date and no playbill. For this one Zylbercweig gives the year, the house, the play and the author. Wikipedia mentions South Africa only in a blanket clause about the 1950s.
stops.quote: In 1955 they traveled with a troupe from Argentina to South Africa (technical college theatre), in Johannesburg with the play, "Mayn gliklekhe heym" by H. Hoffenberg.
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The Technical College Theatre, Johannesburg, and the South African tours mounted out of Buenos Aires
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

segments.name: Israel, the Departure, and the Legal Name of the Arrangement

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the street names called from the hall
stops.date_confidence: The Israeli repertory is cited to Rachel Rojanski's history, citing Maariv of 26 March 1956; neither the monograph nor the newspaper was retrieved. The audience anecdote is Shifra Lerer's own recollection given to Itzik Gottesman in 2011, fifty-five years after the fact, and the Forward piece carrying it was fetched and read directly. It is a recollection, not a contemporaneous report.
stops.campa: He and Lerer play Israel: Yankl der shmid, Gelt, libe un shande, Zayn groyse libe. The state they are performing in has legislated in several ways against Yiddish on its stages, and the halls fill anyway. The people in this one last saw him on a stage in Poland before the war. Lerer's account, given fifty-five years afterward and unsupported by any contemporary notice, is that when he walked out they did not applaud. They called street names at him, the streets they had come from.
stops.quote_source: Shifra Lerer, recalled in Itzik Gottesman, 'Shifra Lerer, 95, Yiddish Star of Stage and Screen,' The Forward, 16 March 2011
suggested_refs: Rachel Rojanski, Yiddish in Israel: A History, on the Yiddish stage under Hebrew-only policy
sources: Itzik Gottesman, The Forward, 16 March 2011
Rachel Rojanski, Yiddish in Israel: A History, citing Maariv, 26 March 1956 (cited, not retrieved)

stops.name: Tel Aviv, leaving on the eve of the Sinai Campaign
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The departure and the press attack rest entirely on Rachel Rojanski's history citing Davar of 8 November 1956; neither the monograph nor the article was retrieved by any researcher on this subject, and no digitized Davar archive was reachable. The claim is specific enough to be treated as likely reliable, and it is not attested independently anywhere.
stops.campa: They leave Israel on the eve of the Sinai Campaign. The Hebrew press turns on them for the timing, most sharply in a Davar piece of the eighth of November headed, in translation, the foreigners stayed and ours fled. This is the one public controversy in his career, and it is a quarrel about Yiddish as much as about a departure date. No official consequence of any kind is recorded. Rojanski's history carries the citations, and the Davar article itself has not been read by anyone working from her.
suggested_refs: Davar, 8 November 1956, and the Israeli press campaign against departing Yiddish performers
sources: Rachel Rojanski, Yiddish in Israel: A History, citing Davar, 8 November 1956 (cited, not retrieved)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Arkhentine Theatre and the marriage
stops.date_confidence: The Argentine engagement is attested by Zylbercweig, who renders the house as the Arkhentine Theatre. The marriage year comes from Wikipedia's Shifra Lerer article and does not depend on the Mount Hebron Cemetery page, which returned a 404. Some later listings give 1956 instead; the discrepancy is minor and unresolved. Coordinate as at the 1946 stop; the Arkhentine is a different house from the Mitre and its address was not established.
stops.campa: He and Lerer guest-star in Argentina again, at the house the lexicon renders as the Arkhentine, and in the same year they marry. They have been a working pair since the Teatro Mitre in 1946 and a single billing since the Public Theatre in 1952. The wedding, eleven years in, changes nothing about the arrangement except its legal name. Some listings give 1956 for it instead and no document settles the point. He is fifty years old and has four years left.
stops.quote: In 1957 both again guest-starred in Argentina in the "Arkhentine" Theatre.
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History
suggested_refs: The Arkhentine (Argentino) Theatre of Buenos Aires, as named in Zylbercweig's entry
sources: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the return two years after the attack
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Rests on a single citation in Rachel Rojanski's history to Herut of 5 June 1958; neither the monograph nor the newspaper item was retrieved. The date is the cited newspaper date, not an established performance date.
stops.campa: Two years after the Davar attack they are back in Israel, playing comedies and musical operettas. Herut reports it on the fifth of June. Whatever the press said in November 1956, no door had been closed: the country that scolded them for leaving books them again the moment they offer to come. The repertory this time is comedies and operettas, the same goods he has been carrying since Vienna. The whole of this rests on one citation in Rojanski's history, and the Herut item behind it has not been retrieved by anyone working on him.
suggested_refs: Herut, 5 June 1958, on the return of Witler and Lerer to the Israeli stage
sources: Rachel Rojanski, Yiddish in Israel: A History, citing Herut, 5 June 1958 (cited, not retrieved)

stops.name: New York, the Farband tour of the United States and Canada
stops.date_confidence: Attested only as a fact, not as a geography. Zylbercweig's whole sentence is that in 1958 both participated in a tour of the Jewish National Workers' Union; no city and no hall is named anywhere. The pin is his New York base, from which such a tour would be mounted, and the month is an ordering device. An earlier draft placed a stop at Montreal's Monument-National on no evidence at all; that placement is withdrawn.
stops.campa: He and Lerer tour the United States and Canada under the Jewish National Workers' Union, the Farband: one-act plays, concerts of folk songs, and songs and duets he has composed himself. The Farband circuit runs through the union's branches in the industrial towns, and he works it as a songwriter as much as an actor. Not one city is named in the record and not one hall. Zylbercweig's whole sentence for the year is that both participated in a tour of the Jewish National Workers' Union.
stops.quote: In 1958 both participated in a tour of the Jewish National Workers' Union.
stops.quote_source: Zalmen Zylbercweig, Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater, vol. 3, English adaptation, Museum of Family History

segments.name: The Records, the Death, and the Boxes at YIVO

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Hed-Arzi and Lomir ale freylekh zayn
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, unresolved. David Assaf dates the Hed-Arzi issue to likely the 1950s; a discographical source cited in the dossier dates a posthumous Hed-Arzi LP, Chansons Populaires Yiddish Vol. 1, catalogue AN 37-33, with a Barclay edition 86009, to February 1962. The two datings are not reconciled and the catalogue entry was not verified against a primary page, the National Library of Israel and WorldCat both refusing the fetch. 1959 is an ordering placement. Coordinate is the Tel Aviv pin for the Israeli label; no studio is named.
stops.campa: Hed-Arzi in Israel issues his songs on record, among them Lomir ale freylekh zayn, let us all be cheerful, credited on the label to him. Its first verse passes into Vizhnitz Hasidic use and is sung at the Purim table, a melody out of a Belz grandson's operetta career coming back into a beis midrash with no one there told where it came from. David Assaf traced the line back as far as the label credit and stopped, because the credit is the last solid thing in the chain.
suggested_refs: David Assaf, Oneg Shabbat, 14 March 2014, on Lomir ale freylekh zayn and its Vizhnitz singing

stops.name: New York, the death with no date on it
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; exact date not established. Wikidata records 1961 at year precision with place given only as the United States. A Forward obituary is cited as of 16 June 1961 and a Hebrew notice in Hadoar, vol. 40 no. 31 p. 559, as of 23 June 1961; neither was retrieved. Zylbercweig cannot be the source for the death, since his volume appeared in 1959. The brain tumour is a retrospective report, not a medical record. Coordinate is the Second Avenue district and is symbolic, not an attested death site.
stops.campa: He dies in the United States in 1961, aged about fifty-four, of a brain tumour according to a report published fifty years afterward. The Forward is said to have run an obituary on the sixteenth of June and Hadoar printed a Hebrew notice on the twenty-third. No exact date has been established. No hospital is named. No burial place has been found: when Lerer dies in 2011 she is laid in Block 67 at Mount Hebron in Flushing beside her second husband, and he is not there. Where his grave is, no source consulted knows.
stops.quote: they married in 1957. Witler died from a brain tumor in 1961.

stops.name: New York, RG 671 at YIVO
stops.date_confidence: The collection is attested: the finding aid is live at yivoarchives.yivo.org, id 33023, and gives RG 671, 3 feet 6 inches, six letter-sized and four legal-sized boxes, 2,100 items, inclusive dates the 1930s to 1961. The accession date is not recorded there, and the date here is an ordering device only. Coordinate is YIVO's own address at 15 West 16th Street; an earlier draft placed it at Columbus Circle, nearly 4 km wrong.
stops.campa: His playscripts go to YIVO, catalogued as RG 671, the Shifra Lerer and Ben-Zion Witler papers: three feet six inches of shelf, ten boxes, some two thousand one hundred items, Yiddish manuscripts, scripts with musical scores, photographs of him, and a scrapbook of his obituaries. The finding aid lists the countries he performed in, and one of them, North Africa, appears nowhere else in any record of his life. There is a tour inside that phrase that nobody has yet gone looking for.
stops.quote: The bulk of the collection is comprised of playscripts including scripts with musical scores
stops.quote_source: YIVO Institute for Jewish Research, finding aid for RG 671, Shifra Lerer and Ben-Zion Witler papers
